terms.gloss: be able to walk there: be within walking distance
evidence: Traupman 171: Pedibus īre possum ad scholam et ad variās tabernās.
Liv. 5.40: sacerdōtēs pūblicās sacraque populī Rōmānī pedibus īre ferrīque
terms.comment: Latin says this with a verb: one can go there on foot. Traupman’s city-dweller gives it as the advantage of living in town. Pedibus īre is the classical phrase for going on foot rather than riding: Livy, of the priestesses and sacred things that had to go on foot, and Plautus, of a slave who wants a chariot sent for him. We have found no noun phrase for “walking distance” in the authors or the reference works we searched.

phrases.latin: Nōn opus est autoraedā; pedibus īrī potest.
phrases.english: We don’t need the car; it’s within walking distance.

phrases.latin: Potestne eō pedibus īrī, an longius abest?
phrases.english: Is it within walking distance, or is it too far?

phrases.latin: Pedibus īre possum ad scholam et ad variās tabernās.
phrases.english: I can walk to school and to the different shops.

phrases.latin: quadrīgās, quī vehar, nam pedibus īre nōn queō
phrases.english: a four-horse chariot to ride in, for I can’t go on foot

sources: Lewis & Short: pes
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 171.
